patient.chief_complaint: DWI restriction on MRI after headache episode — 'confirmed migrainous infarction' — seeking second opinion
patient.hpi:
A 38-year-old Indian-British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for a second opinion following an MRI scan 3 weeks ago. She had an episode 4 weeks ago of visual disturbance in her left peripheral field (shimmering zigzag arc expanding over 20 minutes) followed by a severe right-sided headache lasting 12 hours. When the headache had not fully resolved by day 3, she attended a walk-in clinic, where MRI was arranged. The radiologist reported 'a 4mm area of DWI restriction in the right posterior watershed territory — acute infarction — possible migrainous infarction.' She was started on clopidogrel 75 mg daily and aspirin 75 mg (dual antiplatelet) by the local neurology team who were concerned about migrainous infarction.

She has a 10-year history of migraine with visual aura. She has 2-4 episodes per month, all with typical expanding visual aura over 15-25 minutes followed by right-sided headache. Her neurological symptoms have always been fully reversible after each episode. She had a combined OCP stopped 10 years ago when her migraines were first diagnosed and is now on a progestin-only pill (Cerazette). She is very concerned about the MRI finding and is currently not driving (advised by the previous team).

On review of the MRI images at this clinic: the 4mm DWI lesion is located in the right occipital cortex, and the ADC map shows corresponding low signal (genuine restricted diffusion) — this is a real acute infarction. However, the timing (day 3 post-episode), size, and location require careful interpretation.
pmh: No hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease

medications.indication: Migrainous infarction prevention (started by previous team)
Dual antiplatelet with clopidogrel — requires review

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.1) — small right occipital cortical infarct during established visual aura; all secondary causes excluded; dual antiplatelet needs review (DAPT not indicated long-term)

differential.key_features: No AF on 48-hour Holter; no PFO on echocardiogram; no cardioembolic source identified; infarct size 4mm (typical of migrainous infarction, not embolic); episodic migraine established 10 years; infarct occurred during typical aura
differential.distinguishing_test: Holter (no AF); echocardiogram (no PFO); infarct pattern (small occipital cortical, not embolic territory)

differential.key_features: Antiphospholipid antibodies negative x2 (12-week interval) — APS definitively excluded by two-negative criterion; no prior thrombotic events
differential.distinguishing_test: Antiphospholipid antibodies x2 negative at 12-week interval

differential.key_features: Normal posterior circulation MRA — no PCA stenosis; no vertebral dissection; infarct is small cortical occipital lesion in aura territory; established 10-year migraine history; no embolic source
differential.distinguishing_test: MRA posterior circulation (normal); no embolic source found

optimal_actions.action: Confirm ICHD-3 migrainous infarction diagnosis — small occipital cortical infarct during established visual aura; no other cause found
optimal_actions.expected_finding: 4mm right occipital cortical infarct at 3 days; largely resolved at 4 weeks; normal MRA posterior circulation

optimal_actions.action: Stop clopidogrel — DAPT not indicated for migrainous infarction; aspirin 75 mg monotherapy appropriate
optimal_actions.expected_finding: DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) has no evidence for long-term use in migrainous infarction; aspirin monotherapy appropriate

optimal_actions.action: Initiate strong migraine preventive therapy — topiramate 50-100 mg or propranolol; reducing migraine frequency is primary prevention
optimal_actions.expected_finding: 2-4 attacks/month = preventive therapy strongly indicated; preventing migraine prevents migrainous infarction recurrence

optimal_actions.action: Repeat antiphospholipid antibodies at 12 weeks — confirm APS excluded
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Two negative results 12 weeks apart required for definitive APS exclusion

optimal_actions.action: Driving clearance — 4 weeks post-episode, full recovery, visual fields full; document perimetry and clear patient to drive
optimal_actions.expected_finding: UK DVLA 1-month restriction satisfied; full recovery documented

critical_actions: Confirm ICHD-3 migrainous infarction diagnosis — confirmed DWI restriction in aura territory; all secondary causes excluded
Stop clopidogrel — DAPT not evidence-based for migrainous infarction; aspirin monotherapy appropriate
Migraine prevention is the PRIMARY prevention strategy for migrainous infarction recurrence — initiate topiramate or propranolol
Repeat antiphospholipid antibodies at 12 weeks — required to definitively exclude APS (two negative results needed)
Confirm progestin-only pill is appropriate contraception — combined OCP absolutely contraindicated (already appropriately stopped)
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue dual antiplatelet (DAPT) long-term — no evidence for long-term DAPT in migrainous infarction
Do not prescribe combined OCP — absolute contraindication (already appropriately stopped 10 years ago)
Do not restrict driving beyond 1 month with full neurological recovery — DVLA criteria met at 4 weeks
key_reasoning_points: Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.1) requires: established migraineur; infarction during typical aura; in territory of aura; all secondary causes excluded
The diagnostic puzzle: DWI restriction was present (real infarction) but the previous team added clopidogrel to aspirin — DAPT is not supported by evidence for migrainous infarction
The PRIMARY prevention strategy for migrainous infarction recurrence is preventing the migraine — not anticoagulation
Antiphospholipid antibodies must be repeated at 12 weeks for definitive APS exclusion — a single negative test is insufficient
Cerazette (progestin-only) is appropriate and should be continued — combined OCP was correctly stopped 10 years ago

metadata.condition_name: Confirmed migrainous infarction (real DWI restriction) — DAPT overtreatment, primary prevention through migraine control
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: real DWI-positive infarction creates overtreatment trap (DAPT); recognising migrainous infarction requires excluding all secondary causes; primary prevention is migraine control not anticoagulation

mri.impression: 4 mm area of restricted diffusion in the right occipital cortex — confirmed acute cortical infarction. Corresponding ADC low signal confirms true restriction. No other DWI lesions. Normal posterior circulation MRA — no PCA stenosis or vertebral dissection. Appearances consistent with a small cortical infarction in the right occipital territory. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: migrainous infarction ICHD-3 management antiplatelet DAPT clopidogrel prevention

results.source: ICHD-3; ESO stroke guidelines; Cephalalgia review
results.finding: ICHD-3 1.4.1 migrainous infarction: stroke during migraine aura; infarction in area corresponding to aura; no other stroke cause. Aspirin 75-150 mg daily for secondary prevention (weak evidence; extrapolated from ischaemic stroke). DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel): POINT/CHANCE trials support short-term DAPT for high-risk TIA; for migrainous infarction DAPT benefit unproven — current guidelines do not support long-term DAPT. Combined OCP absolutely contraindicated. Migraine prevention CRITICAL — preventing migraine prevents infarction; topiramate (Level A), propranolol (Level A), anti-CGRP antibodies. Triptans cautioned — weak evidence, individualised decision.
results.evidence_level: ICHD-3 consensus; ESO guidelines; Level A (preventives)

output.summary: For migrainous infarction, aspirin 75-150 mg monotherapy is generally recommended for secondary prevention; long-term DAPT benefit is not established for migrainous infarction; combined OCP is absolutely contraindicated; migraine prevention is the primary strategy to reduce infarction risk; triptans are cautioned based on limited evidence

output.query: triptans migrainous infarction safety contraindication EHF guidelines

results.finding: Triptans are vasoconstrictors; after migrainous infarction, theoretical concern about vasoconstriction in a susceptible territory. No randomised trials specifically address triptan use after migrainous infarction; case reports rare and contradictory. EHF and EFNS caution against triptans but evidence base is weak. Untreated severe migraine attacks cause significant suffering and may trigger further CSD. 2022 EHF guidelines suggest weighing individual risk vs benefit — if infarction was small and well-characterised, cautious triptan use may be acceptable with monitoring. Prioritise strong preventive therapy to reduce acute treatment need.

output.summary: Triptans cautioned (not absolutely contraindicated) after migrainous infarction; prioritise preventive therapy to reduce acute treatment need; shared decision-making

output.query: driving DVLA restrictions migrainous infarction stroke 1 month visual field

results.source: DVLA At a Glance Guide (UK); DVLA medical standards
results.finding: After TIA or stroke with full recovery, DVLA regulations require a 1-month driving cessation period; resumption is permitted when there is no visual field defect on perimetry, no persisting neurological deficit, and no uncontrolled AF. Migrainous infarction is treated as a stroke for DVLA licensing purposes — the 1-month restriction applies. Formal visual field assessment is required before driving resumption is documented.

output.summary: UK DVLA regulations require a 1-month driving cessation after TIA/stroke; resumption requires documented full neurological recovery, no visual field defect on formal perimetry, and no uncontrolled AF; migrainous infarction is classified as a stroke for DVLA purposes
